purpose: Additive teaching fixes under the fast-path process (ADR-0029). Entries only add definitions, analysis dimensions, quantitative methods or named models; they never replace existing teaching. Each fix has one line in content-factory/RUN_LOG.md and every fixed node is checked by the T8 course gate's accuracy question.
rights_boundary: Revision-authored teaching supported by each node's registered promotion-eligible sources. No awarding-body wording.

fixes.run_log: 3.1.1 Profit formula missing

methods.name: Profit
methods.formula: total revenue - total costs, where total costs = fixed costs + total variable costs
methods.worked_example: Revenue £50,000; fixed costs £12,000; variable costs £30,000. Total costs = £42,000, so profit = £50,000 - £42,000 = £8,000.
methods.interpretation: A negative result is a loss. Profit is a measure over a period and is not the same as the cash the business holds.

fixes.run_log: 3.5.1 Return on investment formula not taught

methods.name: Return on investment (ROI)
methods.formula: return from the investment / cost of the investment × 100
methods.worked_example: A £200,000 investment generates £30,000 profit in a year: ROI = £30,000 / £200,000 × 100 = 15% a year.
methods.interpretation: Compares the return with the resources committed. State which return (e.g. profit) and which period are used before comparing options.

fixes.run_log: 3.5.1 Operating profit and profit for the year formulas not taught

definitions: operating profit: gross profit less other operating expenses such as distribution and administrative costs; profit from trading before finance costs and tax
profit for the year: profit remaining after operating profit is reduced by net finance costs and taxation; available to retain in the business or distribute to owners

methods.name: Operating profit
methods.worked_example: Gross profit £400,000; distribution and administrative expenses £250,000. Operating profit = £400,000 - £250,000 = £150,000.
methods.interpretation: Shows how profitable the core trading activity is before financing decisions and tax.

methods.name: Profit for the year
methods.formula: operating profit - net finance costs - taxation
methods.worked_example: Operating profit £150,000; net finance costs £20,000; tax £26,000. Profit for the year = £150,000 - £20,000 - £26,000 = £104,000.
methods.interpretation: The profit attributable to owners for the period; it can be retained or paid out as dividends.

fixes.run_log: 3.5.2 Profit for the year margin formula not taught

methods.name: Profit for the year margin
methods.interpretation: The share of each £1 of revenue left for owners after all costs, interest and tax. Compare with gross and operating margins to see where costs are absorbed.

fixes.run_log: 3.5.2 Break-even chart not taught

definitions: break-even chart: a graph with output on the horizontal axis and costs and revenue on the vertical axis, showing fixed costs, total costs and total revenue; break-even output is where the total revenue and total cost lines cross, and the horizontal distance between actual output and break-even output shows the margin of safety

fixes.run_log: 3.7.2 Statement of financial position not taught as a named statement

definitions: statement of financial position: a statement of a business's assets, liabilities and equity at a single point in time (often called the balance sheet); total assets equal total liabilities plus equity

fixes.run_log: 3.7.2 Payables days, receivables days and inventory turnover formulas not taught

methods.name: Payables days
methods.worked_example: Payables £60,000; cost of sales £730,000. Payables days = £60,000 / £730,000 × 365 = 30 days.
methods.interpretation: Average time taken to pay suppliers. A longer period helps cash flow but can strain supplier relationships or signal payment difficulty.

methods.name: Receivables days
methods.interpretation: Average time customers take to pay. A shorter period improves cash flow; compare with the credit terms the business offers.

methods.name: Inventory turnover
methods.formula: cost of sales / average inventories held
methods.worked_example: Cost of sales £730,000; average inventory £73,000. Inventory turnover = £730,000 / £73,000 = 10 times a year.
methods.interpretation: How many times inventory is used or sold and replaced in a year. Higher usually means inventory moves faster, but a sensible level depends on the industry.

fixes.run_log: 3.5.3 Venture capital missing

definitions: venture capital: equity finance, often with management advice, provided by specialist investors to young or fast-growing businesses with high growth potential in exchange for a share of ownership; it brings expertise but dilutes control and investors expect a high return and an eventual exit

fixes.run_log: 3.2.2 Net gain formula missing

methods.name: Net gain
methods.formula: expected value of an option - cost of that option
methods.worked_example: Option A has an expected value of £500,000 and costs £350,000: net gain = £150,000. Option B has an expected value of £420,000 and costs £250,000: net gain = £170,000, so B has the higher net gain.
methods.interpretation: On financial grounds choose the option with the highest net gain, then weigh the reliability of the probabilities, risk attitude and non-financial factors.

fixes.run_log: 3.3.1 Market size formula not taught

methods.name: Market size
methods.formula: total sales of all firms in the market over a period, measured by value (revenue) or volume (units)
methods.worked_example: Three firms sell £2m, £3m and £5m in a year: market size = £10m by value.
methods.interpretation: Needed for market share and growth calculations. Value and volume can move differently when prices change.

fixes.run_log: 3.4.5 Inventory control chart, re-order quantity and influences on inventory levels missing

definitions: inventory control chart: a graph of inventory level over time showing the maximum inventory level, re-order level, buffer inventory, lead time and re-order quantity
re-order level: the inventory level at which a new order is placed
buffer inventory: the minimum inventory held as protection against unexpected demand or late delivery
lead time: the time between placing an order and receiving it
re-order quantity: the amount ordered each time inventory reaches the re-order level

methods.name: Re-order quantity
methods.worked_example: Maximum inventory 1,000 units and buffer inventory 200 units: re-order quantity = 800 units, so a delivery arriving at the buffer level restores the maximum.
methods.interpretation: Read from an inventory control chart as the vertical jump when a delivery arrives.

methods.name: Re-order level
methods.formula: buffer inventory + (usage per period × lead time in periods)
methods.worked_example: Buffer 200 units, usage 50 units a day, lead time 4 days: re-order level = 200 + (50 × 4) = 400 units.
methods.interpretation: Ordering at this level means the delivery should arrive as inventory falls to the buffer.

analysis_dimensions: influences on inventory levels: demand variability, lead time, supplier reliability, storage and holding costs, perishability or obsolescence, cost of stock-outs and the use of JIT

fixes.run_log: 3.6.2 Employee costs as a percentage of turnover and labour cost per unit formulas missing

methods.name: Employee costs as a percentage of turnover
methods.interpretation: The share of revenue spent on the workforce. A rising figure can mean pay has grown faster than sales or productivity has fallen.

methods.name: Labour cost per unit
methods.formula: total labour costs / units of output
methods.worked_example: Labour costs £300,000 for 60,000 units: labour cost per unit = £5.
methods.interpretation: Falls when productivity rises faster than pay. Compare over time or with competitors producing similar output.

fixes.run_log: 3.10.1 Kotter and Schlesinger methods of overcoming resistance not taught

models_frameworks: Kotter and Schlesinger's methods of overcoming resistance to change
definitions: education and communication: explaining the reasons for change so that people understand it; useful where resistance comes from misunderstanding, but slow with many people
participation and involvement: involving those affected in designing the change; builds commitment but takes time
facilitation and support: training, coaching or emotional support to help people adjust; helps where resistance comes from anxiety, but can be costly and may still fail
negotiation and agreement: offering incentives or concessions in exchange for accepting change; useful where a group clearly loses out, but can be expensive and invite others to negotiate
manipulation and co-option: selectively using information or giving resisters a token role; quick and cheap but can backfire if people feel manipulated
explicit and implicit coercion: forcing change through threats or authority; fast but risks resentment, and best reserved for urgent situations

fixes.run_log: 3.1.1 Social and ethical objectives not taught

definitions: social and ethical objectives: goals a business sets beyond financial return, such as reducing environmental impact, treating staff and suppliers fairly, sourcing ethically or supporting the community; they can strengthen reputation and loyalty but may raise costs or limit profit in the short run

fixes.run_log: 3.1.2 Private limited company, public limited company, private and public sector, not-for-profit and social enterprise not taught

definitions: private limited company (Ltd): an incorporated business, legally separate from its owners, whose shareholders have limited liability; its shares cannot be offered to the general public or traded on a stock exchange, so ownership stays with a small group such as founders, family or chosen investors, which keeps control but limits the capital it can raise

public limited company (plc): an incorporated business with limited liability that is allowed to offer its shares to the public; UK law sets a minimum share capital for a plc and stricter disclosure rules, and a plc may choose to have its shares listed on a stock exchange, which gives access to large amounts of capital but exposes it to takeover and to shareholder pressure

private sector and public sector: private-sector organisations are owned by individuals or shareholders and usually aim to make a profit; public-sector organisations are owned or controlled by central or local government (for example the NHS or local councils) and exist mainly to provide services, funded largely through taxation

not-for-profit organisation: an organisation that does not exist mainly to distribute profit to owners; any surplus is used to pursue its purpose (for example a charity), so success is judged by mission outcomes as well as financial health

social enterprise: a business that trades to achieve a social or environmental purpose and reinvests most of its profits in that purpose rather than paying them to owners; unlike a charity it earns its income mainly by selling goods or services, and unlike a conventional firm it does not aim to maximise owner returns

fixes.run_log: 3.1.3 and 3.7.4/3.7.6 demographic factors, demographic change and migration, consumer lifestyle, online business growth, labour market legislation and government enterprise policy not taught

definitions: demographic factors: measurable characteristics of a population such as its size, age structure, gender balance, household type, geographic spread and ethnic mix; changes in them alter the number and mix of customers and workers a business can draw on (for example an ageing population increases demand for healthcare and reduces the supply of young workers)

demographic change and migration: shifts in birth rates, life expectancy and the movement of people into and out of a country; net migration can add to labour supply and skills and change the pattern of consumer demand, while an ageing population can raise costs for government and employers and change what is bought

consumer lifestyle and buying behaviour: how people live and choose what to buy; trends such as health awareness, concern for sustainability, demand for convenience and use of mobile devices change what customers want, how they search and compare, and where they buy, so businesses must adapt products, promotion and channels

growth of online business: the rise of online retail and digital services, which lowers entry barriers and premises costs, widens reach and lets customers compare prices instantly; it pushes traditional businesses to build a digital presence and rethink stores, delivery and staffing

labour market legislation: laws governing employment, such as the National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage, the Equality Act 2010, working-time rules, health and safety duties and protection from unfair dismissal; they raise costs and compliance duties for employers but protect workers and set a level playing field

government enterprise policy: government measures to encourage new and small businesses, such as start-up loans, grants, tax incentives for investors, advice services and lighter regulation; they lower the risk and cost of starting up, though help is usually limited and may be targeted at particular areas or sectors

fixes.run_log: 3.1.3 Fair trade and 3.7.4 environmental legislation not taught

definitions: fair trade: a trading approach in which producers in developing countries, often farmers, receive a guaranteed minimum price and a premium for community investment, and follow agreed labour and environmental standards; businesses that adopt it can gain ethical appeal and a price premium, but face higher input costs and certification requirements

environmental legislation: laws that limit pollution, emissions and waste, require permits and reporting, and set binding climate targets (for example the UK's Climate Change Act 2008 commits the country to net zero emissions by 2050); compliance can raise costs or force changes to processes, while breaches bring fines and reputational damage

fixes.run_log: 3.2.2 Scientific and intuitive decision making, risk and reward, and influences on decisions not taught

definitions: scientific decision making: a systematic, evidence-based approach in which managers set the objective, gather and analyse relevant data, evaluate the options using techniques such as investment appraisal or decision trees, choose, then review the outcome; it is more objective and defensible but needs time, good data and cost

intuitive decision making: choosing on the basis of experience, judgement and instinct rather than formal analysis; it is fast and useful when time is short, data are scarce or the situation is new, but it is hard to justify and exposed to personal bias and overconfidence

risk and reward in decision making: the benefit a decision could bring weighed against the chance and cost of it going wrong; a business with more resources or a bolder culture may accept higher risk for higher potential reward, while a cautious one prefers safer options

influences on decisions: factors that shape which option managers choose, including the business's mission and objectives, ethics and stakeholder expectations, the external environment such as competition and regulation, and resource constraints such as finance, time and skills

fixes.run_log: 3.3.2 Using marketing data in decisions not taught

definitions: using marketing data in decisions: marketing data from market research and sales records informs decisions such as which segment to target, what price to charge and which products to develop or drop; its value depends on its quality, how representative the sample was and how up to date it is, and it should be used to support judgement rather than replace it

fixes.run_log: 3.3.4 New product development not taught

definitions: new product development (NPD): the process of taking a new product from idea to market, typically idea generation, screening, concept testing, business analysis, development and prototyping, test marketing, launch and review; it helps a business refresh its product portfolio and respond to changing needs, but is costly and many new products fail

fixes.run_log: 3.3.4 Social media promotion, viral marketing and e-commerce not taught

definitions: social media promotion: using platforms such as Instagram, TikTok or LinkedIn to share paid and unpaid content, work with influencers and target adverts at chosen groups; it is relatively cheap, measurable and allows two-way contact with customers, but results are hard to control and negative comments can spread quickly

viral marketing: a message or piece of content that customers choose to pass on to others, so that it spreads rapidly through their networks at little cost to the business; it can deliver large reach cheaply but its success is unpredictable and the message cannot be controlled once shared

e-commerce: buying and selling goods and services over the internet, through a business's own website or app or through online marketplaces; it extends reach beyond a local area, is open at all hours and gives useful customer data, but requires investment in delivery, payment security and returns, and exposes the business to intense price comparison

fixes.run_log: 3.4.1 Added value not taught

definitions: added value: the difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials and services used to make it (for example a product sold for £50 using £30 of bought-in inputs adds £20 of value); businesses add value by design, quality, service or branding, and higher added value supports higher margins

fixes.run_log: 3.4.3 Just in case and 3.4.5 matching supply to demand, temporary and part-time staff and producing to order not taught

definitions: just in case (JIC): an inventory approach in which a business holds buffer stocks so that it can meet unexpected demand or cope with supply delays; it reduces the risk of stock-outs but ties up cash and storage space and risks waste, in contrast to just in time

matching supply to demand: adjusting what the business can supply to what customers want, using forecasting, buffer inventory, flexible capacity, flexible staffing and scheduling; poor matching causes either lost sales and waiting customers or costly unsold stock and idle capacity

temporary and part-time staff: workers employed for limited periods or fewer hours, used to cover seasonal peaks or uneven demand; they let a business match labour supply to demand and avoid paying for idle time, but may be less committed and trained and can have high turnover

producing to order: starting production only when a customer has placed an order (also called make to order); it keeps finished stock and waste low and suits bespoke products, but customers wait longer and the business must have flexible capacity

fixes.run_log: 3.4.3 Labour-intensive versus capital-intensive production not taught

definitions: labour-intensive and capital-intensive production: a labour-intensive process relies mainly on people (for example a consultancy or hairdresser) so labour is the largest cost, while a capital-intensive process relies mainly on machinery and equipment (for example a car plant) so the largest costs are fixed; labour-intensive methods are usually more flexible and suit personalised work, capital-intensive methods can deliver lower unit costs at high volume but need heavy investment

fixes.run_log: 3.6.3 Product-based and regional structures, and 3.10.1 flexible organisations, delayering and flexible contracts not taught

definitions: product-based structure: an organisation divided into units according to the products or product ranges it sells, each with its own managers and often its own functions; it builds product expertise and accountability, but duplicates roles and can cause rivalry and inconsistency between units

regional structure: an organisation divided by geographical area, each region managed with some independence; it responds to local customers and conditions and suits international firms, but can duplicate functions and make central coordination and consistency harder

delayering: removing one or more layers from the hierarchy, which widens spans of control and shortens chains of command; it cuts cost and speeds communication, but increases managers' workloads and may cause job losses and loss of promotion routes

flexible organisation: an organisation able to change quickly in response to shifts in demand or the environment, for example through multi-skilled staff, flatter structures, outsourcing and a mix of permanent core staff and flexible peripheral workers; it improves responsiveness and controls cost, but can reduce job security and employee loyalty

flexible employment contracts: arrangements other than standard full-time permanent jobs, such as part-time, temporary, fixed-term, zero-hours and freelance contracts; they help the employer match labour to demand and control costs, but may bring less commitment, higher turnover and concerns about security for workers

fixes.run_log: 3.6.3 Redeployment and redundancy not taught

definitions: redeployment: moving an employee to a different role, department or location within the same business, often with retraining, for example when a role is no longer needed; it keeps skills and avoids redundancy costs, but the new job may be a poor fit or less attractive to the employee

redundancy: ending an employee's job because the role is no longer needed, for instance after restructuring, falling demand or automation, rather than because of the employee's conduct; employees with enough service are entitled to statutory redundancy pay and employers must consult, so redundancy cuts costs but brings payment costs, lower morale and loss of skills

fixes.run_log: 3.6.4 Empowerment, flexible working and job rotation not taught

definitions: empowerment: giving employees more authority to make decisions and take responsibility for their own work; it can raise motivation, because it offers responsibility and recognition, and speed up decisions, but needs training and trust and can lead to inconsistent decisions or mistakes

flexible working: arrangements that give employees choice over when, where or how long they work, such as flexitime, remote working, compressed hours and job sharing; it can improve work-life balance, retention and recruitment, but can make coordination, supervision and cover harder

job rotation: moving employees between different tasks or roles of a similar level for set periods; it reduces boredom, builds a wider range of skills and gives cover for absence, but costs training time and may lower productivity in the short run

fixes.run_log: 3.6.5 Employee involvement and 3.10.2 reasons for and problems of changing culture not taught

definitions: employee involvement: giving employees a say in decisions that affect them, through consultation, suggestion schemes, team briefings, quality circles or employee representatives; UK regulations can require larger employers to inform and consult employees where enough of them ask; involvement builds commitment and uses employees' knowledge, but slows decisions and can raise expectations that are not met

reasons for and problems of changing culture: a business may need to change its culture because of a new strategy, a merger, poor performance, new leadership or a changed environment; culture change is difficult because values and habits are deeply held, it takes years, it can meet resistance, and staff may leave if they do not accept the new way of working

fixes.run_log: 3.7.1 Corporate objectives, functional objectives and short-termism not taught

definitions: corporate objectives: the overall goals of the whole business, such as profit growth, market share or survival, set by senior managers and the board in line with the mission; they set the direction for strategy and for every department

functional objectives: goals set for a particular department such as marketing, operations, finance or human resources, designed to support the corporate objectives; objectives need to be consistent across functions, or departments can pull in different directions

short-termism: giving priority to short-term results such as quarterly profit or the share price at the expense of long-term investment in areas like research, training or sustainability; it can be driven by shareholder pressure and bonus schemes and may damage the business's long-term competitiveness

fixes.run_log: 3.7.3 Core competences and 3.8.2 price and non-price competition not taught

definitions: core competences: the main skills, knowledge and capabilities that give a business its competitive advantage and that competitors find hard to copy, such as a distinctive technology, design capability or logistics expertise; they can often be applied to several products or markets

price competition and non-price competition: price competition means winning customers mainly by charging less than rivals, which suits low-cost producers in price-sensitive markets but squeezes margins; non-price competition means winning customers through quality, design, branding, service, convenience or innovation, which can support higher prices but costs money to sustain

fixes.run_log: 3.7.4 Competition law not taught

definitions: competition law: laws that protect competition in markets, in the UK chiefly the Competition Act 1998, which prohibits anti-competitive agreements such as price fixing and cartels and abuse of a dominant position, and the Enterprise Act 2002, under which mergers can be investigated; the Competition and Markets Authority enforces them and can impose heavy fines, so firms must consider legal limits when setting prices, agreeing with rivals or growing by merger

fixes.run_log: 3.7.5 GDP not taught

definitions: GDP (gross domestic product): the total value of goods and services produced within a country in a period, usually a year; growth in real GDP (adjusted for inflation) signals rising output and incomes, which usually lifts demand for many products, while falling GDP points to recession; GDP per head helps compare living standards but does not show how income is shared or capture unpaid work or environmental cost

fixes.run_log: 3.8.1 Influences on choice of markets and products not taught

definitions: influences on choice of markets and products: factors that shape where a business competes and what it sells, including market size and growth, the strength of competition, customer needs, the business's own resources and capabilities, its objectives and appetite for risk, and external factors such as regulation and the economy; a choice that looks attractive in the market may still be wrong if the business lacks the resources to succeed

fixes.run_log: 3.9.1 Economies of scope not taught

definitions: economies of scope: cost savings achieved by producing or selling a range of related products together, because they share resources such as premises, equipment, distribution, marketing or brand, so that the cost of the range is lower than making each product separately; they differ from economies of scale, which come from increasing the output of one product

fixes.run_log: 3.9.2 Product innovation, patents, copyright and pressures for innovation, and 3.9.4 e-commerce (strategic) not taught

definitions: product innovation: developing new or significantly improved products, as opposed to process innovation, which improves how things are made; it can create competitive advantage and new revenue but needs investment and carries a high risk of failure

patent: a legal right, granted on application, giving an inventor the exclusive right to make and sell a new invention for up to 20 years; it protects the return on research spending but requires public disclosure and lapses after expiry, when rivals may copy the invention

copyright: automatic legal protection for original creative works such as writing, music, images, software and film, which stops others copying them without permission; no registration is needed in the UK and protection for most works lasts for the author's lifetime plus 70 years

pressures for innovation: forces that push a business to innovate, including competitive pressure from rivals' new products, changing customer tastes, technological change, the decline of existing products and regulation such as environmental rules; a business that does not respond risks losing market share

e-commerce as a strategic choice: moving some or all of a business's selling and operations online can change its business model, reach, cost structure and supply chain and enables use of customer data; it needs long-term investment in technology, delivery and security, and risks conflict with existing channels such as shops

fixes.run_log: 3.10.1 Restructuring and knowledge and information management not taught

definitions: restructuring: making a major change to the way a business is organised, for example by delayering, merging departments, closing or relocating sites or changing product focus; it can cut costs and improve fit with strategy, but brings redundancy costs, disruption and lower morale

knowledge and information management: the way a business captures, stores, shares and uses what it knows, including data, records and employees' experience, through systems such as databases and intranets and through routines for sharing know-how; good management supports decisions and change, while poor management causes duplicated effort, overload, loss of knowledge when staff leave and data protection risks

fixes.run_log: 3.2.1 Democratic and laissez-faire leadership labels not taught

definitions: democratic leadership: the leader involves the team in decisions, by consulting or voting before deciding; it is the participative style. It can raise commitment and use employees' ideas, but decisions are slower and it suits poorly in a crisis or when staff lack the skill or information to contribute

laissez-faire leadership: the leader leaves the team to make decisions and organise its own work with little direction; it is the free-rein style. It suits skilled, self-motivated teams and can encourage creativity, but can cause lack of direction, inconsistent decisions and weak accountability if staff are inexperienced

fixes.run_log: 3.3.4 Penetration pricing and price skimming not taught

definitions: penetration pricing: setting a low price at launch to win market share quickly, often for a new product in a price-sensitive market; it can build volume and deter rivals, but profit per unit is low at first and raising the price later may lose customers

price skimming: setting a high price at launch for a new or innovative product, aimed at customers willing to pay a premium, then lowering the price over time; it earns high margins early and helps recover development costs, but sells low volumes at first and can attract competitors into the market

fixes.run_log: 3.3.4 Physical environment in the service marketing mix not taught

definitions: physical environment (physical evidence): the look, layout and atmosphere of the place where a service is delivered, and other tangible cues such as a website, uniform or packaging; because a service is intangible, customers use these cues to judge quality, so they shape the customer experience and must fit the rest of the mix, for example a premium price with a shabby environment sends mixed signals

fixes.run_log: 3.4.2 Labour productivity taught only per labour hour, not output per employee

definitions: labour productivity (output per employee): output in a period divided by the number of employees in that period; this is the standard measure used for A-level calculations, and output per labour hour is a related measure that should be labelled as such

methods.name: Labour productivity (output per employee)
methods.formula: output per period / number of employees
methods.worked_example: A bakery makes 12,000 loaves in a month with 24 employees: 12,000 / 24 = 500 loaves per employee per month. If output rises to 13,500 loaves with the same 24 employees, productivity = 13,500 / 24 = 562.5 loaves per employee, a rise of 12.5%.
methods.interpretation: Higher output per employee means lower labour cost per unit if pay is unchanged, but the figure ignores hours worked and the quality of the output.

fixes.run_log: 3.6.2 Labour productivity taught only per labour hour, not output per employee

definitions: labour productivity as an HR performance measure: output per period divided by the number of employees; a rise can reflect better training, motivation, job design or technology, and a fall can signal low morale, poor skills or under-used staff

methods.name: Labour productivity (HR measure, output per employee)
methods.formula: output per period / number of employees
methods.worked_example: A call centre handles 18,000 customer calls in a month with 60 employees: 18,000 / 60 = 300 calls per employee. After training, it handles 19,800 calls with 60 employees: 19,800 / 60 = 330 calls per employee, up 10%.
methods.interpretation: Compare across periods or against similar businesses; read it alongside labour turnover and absenteeism, because a rise bought by overwork may not last.

fixes.run_log: 3.5.2 Income, expenditure and profit budgets not taught

definitions: income budget: the planned revenue or other income for a period, for example expected sales by product or month
expenditure budget: the planned spending for a period, for example costs of materials, wages and overheads, often set for each department or cost centre

profit budget: the planned profit for a period, found by subtracting budgeted expenditure from budgeted income; it brings the income and expenditure budgets together and is the figure actual results are compared with

methods.name: Budgeted profit
methods.worked_example: Income budget £200,000; expenditure budget £165,000. Profit budget = £200,000 - £165,000 = £35,000. If actual income is £190,000 and expenditure £160,000, actual profit is £30,000, a £5,000 adverse profit variance.
methods.interpretation: Variances on the income and expenditure budgets explain the variance on the profit budget.

fixes.run_log: 3.6.1 Employee engagement, diversity and alignment of values not taught

definitions: employee engagement: how committed and enthusiastic employees are about their work and the business, beyond simply turning up; engaged employees tend to show higher productivity and lower absence and turnover, and engagement is encouraged by involvement, recognition, development and good leadership

workforce diversity: differences between employees in characteristics such as age, gender, ethnicity, disability, background and skills; in the UK the Equality Act 2010 prohibits discrimination based on protected characteristics, and a diverse workforce can bring wider ideas and better understanding of customers, but needs managing through communication, training and inclusive practice

alignment of values: how closely employees' own values match the business's stated values and culture; close alignment supports commitment, teamwork and consistent behaviour, while a mismatch can cause conflict, low morale and staff leaving

fixes.run_log: 3.6.5 Trade unions not taught

definitions: trade union: an organisation of workers that represents its members' interests to employers; it negotiates pay and conditions through collective bargaining, supports members in disciplinary and grievance cases, and can organise industrial action after a ballot of members. For employees it gives a stronger collective voice and protection; for employers it gives one channel for consultation and agreement, but can make change slower and industrial action can disrupt operations. A union represents employees from outside the business, unlike a works council, which is an internal consultative body

fixes.run_log: 3.6.4 Salary and team working as motivation methods not taught

definitions: salary: a fixed annual payment, usually paid monthly regardless of hours worked or output; it gives employees security and helps attract and retain staff, but does not itself reward extra effort and is a fixed cost to the business

team working: organising employees into groups that share tasks, goals and responsibility; it can meet social needs, combine skills and raise motivation through belonging and shared success, but can cause conflict, free-riding and slower decisions, and needs clear goals and good leadership

fixes.run_log: 3.7.1 Influences on mission not taught

definitions: influences on mission: a business's mission is shaped by who owns it and what the owners value (for example a social enterprise or a shareholder-owned company), the founder's values, stakeholder expectations, the stage the business has reached, its financial position, and external factors such as competition, technology, law and social attitudes; because mission is a broad long-term statement of purpose, these influences usually change its emphasis gradually, and a change of owner, a crisis or a new market can prompt a rewrite

fixes.run_log: 3.7.4 Infrastructure not taught

definitions: infrastructure: the basic physical and organisational systems an economy relies on, such as roads, rail, ports, airports, broadband and mobile networks, and energy and water supply; good infrastructure lowers transport and communication costs, makes supply chains more reliable and widens access to markets and workers, so it influences where businesses locate and invest, while poor infrastructure such as slow broadband or congested roads raises costs, causes delays and can deter investment. Businesses cannot control it, so they must plan around it, and its importance differs between, for example, an online retailer and a manufacturer that exports

fixes.run_log: 3.10.1 Internal and external causes of change, and incremental versus disruptive change not taught

definitions: internal causes of change: pressures arising inside the business, such as new leadership, poor performance, a new strategy or objectives, growth, a change in culture, or new technology the business decides to adopt; these can often be planned and timed by the business

external causes of change: pressures arising outside the business, such as competitor actions, economic conditions, changing customer tastes, new technology in the market, legislation, and social and environmental pressure; the business cannot control these, so change is often a reaction and may be urgent

incremental change: a series of small, gradual adjustments to existing ways of working; it is lower risk, meets less resistance and is easier to manage, but may be too slow when conditions shift quickly

disruptive change: a sudden, large-scale break from existing ways of working, such as a major restructure, a new business model or a response to a crisis; it can deliver large gains quickly but brings high cost, uncertainty and resistance. It should not be confused with disruptive technology, which is one possible trigger

fixes.run_log: 3.10.4 Evaluating strategic performance and the value of strategic planning not taught

definitions: evaluating strategic performance: judging how far a strategy achieved its objectives by comparing results with targets (for example sales, market share, profit or ROCE), looking at trends over time, benchmarking against competitors and using customer and employee measures; a sound judgement allows for external conditions, the time a strategy takes to pay off, and trade-offs between short-term and long-term results, and reaches a conclusion that depends on stated criteria

value of strategic planning: planning gives direction, aligns functions, helps allocate resources, sets targets for control and prepares for risk; its limits are that plans rely on forecasts that may be wrong, take time and cost, and can make a business inflexible or slow to spot opportunities that emerge; planning adds most value when the environment is fairly predictable, the decisions are costly to reverse, and plans are reviewed and supported by contingency planning
